Case study · Escalation · Partner Retention
Reputation and renewal risk management
A reputational escalation was managed by aligning internal stakeholders, addressing client concerns, and protecting both the renewal of a convention and the partner relationship.
Escalation Crisis Management Partner Retention Communication Control Compliance Claims Resolution
Context
A partner university escalated a complaint after a student received payment reminders, legal notices, and summonses relating to unpaid medical invoices. The former client, as no longer insured with us, then posted across several social media platforms, using highly critical language to denounce the service, state that no payment had been made, claim that no response had been received, and accuse the insurance of fraud.
Risks
Hover over a petal to read each risk
Approach
The first priority was to close the communication loop and regain control of the case. The student was raising the issue simultaneously through multiple channels: the university contact, the insurance helpline, and direct contact with us. This created fragmented information and inconsistent versions of the same issue.

A legal derogation signed by the client was confirmed on file to authorize information sharing with the university contact, as the insurer was otherwise not permitted to disclose medical information to that person.

A single point of contact was then designated on each side to ensure that all parties worked from the same information. Both systems were updated so that all communications, whether by email or phone, were routed through the designated contacts only.
A video call was organized with the client, her university representative, the insurer, and me in my role as broker, to address the complaint, reset expectations, and bring all stakeholders onto a single communication channel.

The written exchanges had been fragmented, with missing invoice references, limited supporting documentation, and highly derogatory language towards the teams. During the call, it was agreed that I would act as the broker’s sole point of contact for the case, that any communication sent directly to the insurer would be systematically redirected to me, and that I would be the only person providing the client with updates.

The client was also reminded that, in line with the policy terms and applicable Swiss regulations, it was her responsibility as claimant to provide the information requested by the insurer in order for the claim review to proceed.

Clear next steps and deadlines were confirmed to maintain momentum and support an effective resolution.
Working with the insurer team, a consolidated claims tracker covering over 200 claims was completed to provide a full view of the claim adjudication history, including paid, partially paid, declined, and pending items, together with the relevant claim details.

The review showed that the invoices the student was disputing had never in fact been received. It also confirmed that a small number of invoices managed by recovery agencies had initially been declined correctly in line with the policy terms and conditions.

The insurer prioritized the open invoices that had never been received and processed them within 24 hours. Those invoices, along with the previously declined recovery-agency items, were then paid as a commercial gesture to bring the matter to resolution.

The premium refund remained pending receipt of the bank details required to process the prorated reimbursement for the covered period prior to cancellation, which had been requested on several occasions.
Outcome
The case was successfully closed, the convention was signed, and the university contacted us to express its appreciation for the professionalism and effectiveness shown in resolving the complaint. The structured handling of the matter helped protect the university relationship and preserve trust in a highly sensitive context.
Key insight
Sensitive cases require one clear point of contact, control of the communication flow, and transparency to reestablish trust.
Case study · TPA Onboarding · Network Management
Onboarding of a new TPA
A TPA onboarding project combining provider selection and operational design to ensure a smooth service transition and access to outpatient direct billing.
TPA Onboarding Direct Billing OP Operational Integration Service Transition
Context
A VIP client raised a concern about unequal access to care
A VIP client raised a concern about expatriated employees and the unequal access to care depending on the country of assignment. The issue was not so much direct billing for in-patient treatment, but the lack of direct billing for out-patient care. This created inconsistency across employee populations and raised concerns about duty of care.
Italy: volume too limited for a direct network
The request focused on Italy. From a market perspective, the employee population was too limited and too dispersed to justify building a direct medical network on our own. There was not enough volume to create strong negotiation leverage with providers, nor enough frequency to ensure that a direct procedure would remain sustainable over time if turnover changed. As a result, working through a TPA specialised in the Italian market was the most cost-effective and sustainable solution.
An opportunity to benchmark and improve
It was also an opportunity to review the existing TPA solution and benchmark it against others to assess whether the setup could be improved, whether it met the requirements, and what the cost of the services would be.
Approach
Aligned all impacted teams around the change requested, kept the client informed of each key stage, and built a project plan with clear deadlines, dependencies, and parallel workstreams.

Negotiated the service scope, the fees and involved finance and legal to secure guarantees, review contractual terms, and define the working capital fund. In parallel, the operational model was designed with SOPs, escalation points, delegation rules, and SLAs.

Client requirement met

Case study · Retention Strategy · Student IPMI
A scalable retention strategy for the student IPMI portfolio
A scalable retention strategy for a compliance-driven student insurance portfolio, built on service quality, regulatory expertise, and tailored partner support.
Retention Service Design Regulatory Compliance B2B2C
Context
Individual product, collective distribution
The student solution was sold as an individual product but distributed through universities, private schools, and companies, where student affairs teams and HR often acted as the operational interface. In practice, this created a collective-client model requiring a client relationship manager to manage renewals, operational coordination, and exemption-related escalations.
A regulated environment requiring genuine expertise
Switzerland’s regulatory framework added further complexity: foreign students had to be insured from day one and prove coverage with an authorized insurer. If they could not, they were automatically affiliated to a Swiss LAMal insurer, which is typically more expensive and offers less suitable coverage for their needs.

They also had to apply for exemption from compulsory health insurance through the relevant cantonal authority. Because rules varied by student profile and canton, service quality, regulatory expertise, and local knowledge were central to the customer experience.
Challenge & Objective
CHALLENGE 1
Schools often struggled to explain insurance eligibility, terminology, and exemption requirements clearly to international students.
CHALLENGE 2
In several cantons, the exemption process remained paper-based, creating repeated questions, delayed submissions, and a significant administrative burden for student affairs teams.
CHALLENGE 3
In a market with limited product differentiation, retention depended primarily on service quality and the ability to create added value.
OBJECTIVE
Enhance our services and adapt them to the client’s needs, population, and internal structure — through data and dashboards, day-to-day queries, visits, renewal periods, and patterns observed in specific cantons.
Approach

A structured retention strategy was put in place to reduce friction for schools, improve the student experience, and strengthen partner relationships across onboarding, exemption handling, on-site support, and renewal. The approach was designed to be scalable, with a clear schedule of webinars, campus presence, tailored communication, and data-based renewal presentations based on the school data vs the full portfolio.

Click any step to read about it
Outcome
The approach reduced the administrative burden for schools, reinforced our position as the main point of contact for insurance matters, and strengthened our role as a trusted partner. It also improved responsiveness, supported the school’s duty of care, and helped shift enrolments earlier in the cycle, with webinar-led communications moving peak enrolments to before arrival in Switzerland.
Key insight
In regulated markets where product differentiation is limited, retention is built through the service model: clarity, consistency, and proximity matter as much as cover.
Case study · Data Strategy · Insurer Negotiation
Data-Driven Renewal Strategy for an IPMI Student Solution
A data-driven renewal strategy for a student insurance portfolio that strengthened partner relationships, maintained commercial competitiveness, and identified new commercial opportunities.
Data-Driven Renewal Retention Partner Relations Product Innovation
Context
A white-label IPMI student solution distributed across 26 Swiss cantons
This case concerned the annual renewal of a white-label IPMI student solution with Allianz Care, distributed across the 26 cantons in Switzerland. As the solution expanded, the strategic focus shifted toward stronger results and premium competitiveness in a highly competitive market.
A broader partnership requiring a win-win approach
The negotiation took place within a broader partnership, with multiple contracts already in place and the student portfolio representing the first renewal of the season. As it was not the largest contract, it was important to protect the long-term relationship and avoid jeopardizing future renewal discussions for the main portfolios. The approach was therefore based on a win-win mindset, aiming for a mutually beneficial agreement.
Challenge
Premium competitiveness
The main challenge was to keep premiums competitive while facing aggressive competitor pricing.
Regulatory & compliance constraints
Regulatory and compliance constraints limited the ability to adjust benefits or redesign the solution.
Limited risk-management flexibility
The contract structure also limited risk-management flexibility, and the portfolio was not performing as strongly as expected for a young population.
Claims concentrated in Switzerland
Claims were mainly concentrated in Switzerland, where medical care is among the most expensive in the market.
Market Research — Benefits, Services & Premiums Comparison

Before starting the portfolio performance analysis, a comparison of benefits and services as well as benchmarking across competing student IPMI solutions was carried out. This ensured that any premium positioning was grounded not only in price but in what each solution actually delivered — identifying where our offer was stronger, equivalent, or weaker relative to the market.

Data & Analysis
Portfolio performance reviewed using the insurer’s actuarial analysis: age & demographic profile, high-cost claims, claims trends, most used benefits, geographical distribution, reimbursed amounts, loss ratio, and performance by deductible and segment.
Rather than a blanket increase, a segmented renewal approach with 12 segments was proposed — based on age bracket, solution chosen, and deductible level. More precise and better aligned with the actual risk profile of the portfolio.
Illustrative example of the segmentation approach. Figures are not the actual renewal values.

Although the scheme was collective, enrolment was individual. The systematic collection of school name at enrolment was introduced via web-based forms stored in the GED system — improving visibility across the distribution network.

This allowed us to identify:
→ Which schools generated the most students each year.
→ Which plan was most chosen by students.
→ Which deductible was most selected.
→ Which age brackets were most represented.

Process Automation – Risk Reduction – Provider Network
Turning invoice management into a GED-driven operating model
Antaé · Montreux · 2016–2019
DMAIC GED / EDM TPA Model
Context
During a meeting about a three-year contract renewal, we met with the client's decision makers, finance leaders, and operational teams, including student affairs and nurses. The client was satisfied with the insurance and medical assistance solution itself, including the insurer, premium, and service offer.

The concern came from the operational teams, who flagged issues with medical invoices being sent directly to students or the school on campus. Unlike a local Swiss insurer, the international model did not consistently support direct billing for outpatient care, and students often had to pay providers upfront because the insurer was not always recognized. The problem was not whether the invoices would be paid, but how they were received and handled within the operational flow between provider, student, and insurer.

In practice, the existing glocal model was not performing well enough operationally.

Local providers re-engaged; school teams relieved from invoice follow-up.
Cost-containment model established
Structured provider network improved long-term portfolio management and reduced inefficiencies.
Scalable model with lasting impact
A recurring pain point turned into a scalable model with lasting impact on service quality and cost control.
Key insight
The real value of the project was not only solving an invoice-processing problem, but building a scalable operational model that aligned client expectations, provider requirements, and long-term cost control. By structuring a local provider network and improving invoice governance, Antaé turned a recurring pain point into a strategic market advantage.
TPA Onboarding – Direct Billing – Operational Integration
Provider network upload standardization
April International Care France · Paris · 2020–2022
TPA Onboarding Direct Billing OP Operational Integration Service Transition
Context
A CSM system and client-facing app were already in place to help members find in-network providers, but provider data updates remained manual. Although bulk upload automation was already on the IT roadmap, a VIP tender with a short deadline accelerated the project so the full medical network could be presented to the client. The goal was to translate business requirements into a structured process for cleaning, mapping, and uploading provider network data.
Challenges
Uncharted territory
  • The bulk upload had never been attempted before
  • Uncertainty about whether it would work and whether the CSM system could support such a high volume of providers
  • The file format had to be defined, created, and tested from the ground up
Data quality & fragmentation
  • Provider data came from multiple sources in different formats
  • Needed to be cleaned, standardised, and made usable in both backend and app
  • Duplicates, incomplete records, and ghost providers to remove
Approach — 7 phases
Outcome
VIP tender supported
Fully operational provider network in the app, enabling the client to see the network in real time.
Bulk upload live
5,000+ providers integrated, improving data quality and usability across backend and member app.
Repeatable framework
Standardised, documented process replicable by future teams without starting from scratch.
Patient steering enabled
Preferred network steers members toward conventions and negotiated discounts, improving cost containment.
Key insight
The real challenge was not the upload itself, but designing the rules, structure, and governance needed for the network to work in both the backend and the app.

Cross-Functional – Process Mapping – US Market – Operational Alignment
Project Simply America — US Corridor Operational Model
April International Care France – Paris – 2022–2024
Cross-functional Leadership Process Mapping US TPA Management Case Management High-Cost Claims Governance
Context — the most complex market in the portfolio
The US corridor was the most operationally complex and financially sensitive part of the portfolio.

The American healthcare system — with its PPO networks, CVS/Caremark set up, CPT and DRG billing codes, and in-network/out-of-network cost differentials — operates differently from IPMI markets we might be more used to.

Paris, Mexico, and the US TPA were working in silos, which created mistrust, confusion over responsibilities, gaps in service quality, inconsistent handling of high-cost cases and poor coordination across the customer and claims lifecycle.
Challenge
Sales & Onboarding
  • Product not always understood and explained correctly to the client
  • No standardized onboarding process for new clients
  • Setup delays reduced onboarding efficiency and delayed access to care, direct billing, and client satisfaction
Teams Coordination
  • Key operational flows not clearly owned or understood
  • Lack of a shared view across teams
  • Mistrust between teams affecting day-to-day collaboration
Case & Claims Handling
  • Pharmacy card and PPO network not well integrated in practice
  • Open invoices not consistently reconciled between entities
  • No clear escalation path for complex or high-cost cases
Cost & Resilience
  • High-cost claims not subject to a structured review process
  • BCP mapping incomplete — operational resilience at risk
  • Members not systematically steered toward lower-cost care options
Approach — two years, three teams, end-to-end
Outcomes
Operational dialogue restored
Paris, Mexico, and the US TPA moved from siloed working to a shared follow-the-sun model.
Clearer US operating model
Documented workflows and responsibilities helped each team work more effectively.
Better case handling
Improved coordination reduced case management gaps and improved member service consistency.
High-cost claims governance
Structured review process aligned with insurer regulations for the most financially exposed claims.
Stronger operational resilience
BCP mapping and critical flows updated, database maintained, reducing operational risk.
Improved care navigation
Member communications and team training improved guidance on coverage and the US healthcare system.
Key insight
The portfolio's biggest challenge was not the US market itself, but the lack of a shared operating model around it. Once roles, flows, data, governance, training, and member guidance were aligned, service quality and cost control improved together.
